name: Squirrel Grey
lede: Squirrel Grey is a bluish gray first dated by Ridgway in 1912, close enough to the everyday word Grey that the two are hard to tell apart on screen.

sections.title: A 1912 animal word
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 standard places this hue on plate XLIX, and the 1955 ISCC-NBS system classes it as a bluish gray, block 186 [1]. The RAL paint system also carries an approximate screen match at RAL 7000 [1]. Unlike the slate and taupe colors in this library, Squirrel Grey is not grouped with other named variants; it stands on the animal's coat alone [1].

The nearest everyday name on file is plain [[grey]], only 4.6 units of CIEDE2000 away, a close match [1]. [[slate-grey]], [[charcoal]] and [[silver]] are the other names that turn up far more often than chance in paintings that also carry this color [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a close match to Squirrel Grey in 564 of 23,781 paintings, about 2.4 percent, as photographed [2]. It plays a highlight slightly more often than a midtone, 54 percent against 41 percent [2]. Salomon van Ruysdael, Bernardo Bellotto and Vincent van Gogh all use it well above the archive's average rate, with Peder Severin Krøyer's 1899 *Boys Bathing at Skagen* its strongest single match [2].

The earliest dated match is a 1430 Madonna and Child attributed to Bicci di Lorenzo, five centuries before Ridgway's plate, which only shows a similar screen color was photographed there, not that the name existed that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
